bull_bear.title: Non-obvious takeaways

bull_bear.body:
- Buyback announced in April 2026 of "Rs. 180 Crs." for "1 Cr. Equity Shares proposed for Buyback representing 3.67% of total paid up capital" at "Rs. 180 per Equity Share"; the Chairman states it "got concluded during the quarter".
- "Members of the promoter and promoter group of the Company have indicated their intention not to participate in the proposed Buyback", which the MD frames as ensuring "the full benefit flowed to our public shareholders" and the deck frames as "signaling strong long-term conviction in the business".
- Balance sheet: "As of today, we are fully debt-free and clear of all legacy CDR obligations"; the historical section is headed "We are a NET CASH Company", and the journey notes "Net cash positive by FY22; (Zero Debt Company - Out of CDR Scheme)".
- Legacy CDR settlement: "The Company honored its Right of Recompense (RoR) with payments aggregating to Rs. 101 crore to consortium lenders"; the deck states total provisions of Rs. 50.6 crore comprising Rs. 32.0 crore in FY24 and Rs. 18.6 crore in FY25, with a footnote that "the remaining 49.2 crore has been recognized in Q4 FY26".
- The buyback is framed as "the first of many steps in returning value to shareholders in a business with a much cleaner capital structure".
bull_bear.title: Capital allocation policy (investor deck)

bull_bear.body:
- One of the key suppliers of bearing rings in India, supplying most of the leading bearing companies, and a Tier-1 supplier to global manufacturers of automotive assemblies
- Largest forging capacity in India by the Company's own description, and ranked 5th largest in India by installed forging capacity, with combined installed forging capacity of 1,65,000 MTPA
- Well-invested manufacturing infrastructure combining multiple high-speed hot formers from Sakamura, Hatebur, Enomoto, Eumuco and Kurimoto, with machining lines of CNC/VMC spindles from Mori Seiki, DMG, FUJI, Hyundai, Mazak, Muratec, ACE and TSUGAMI
- Scale in machining with 625 CNC/VMC spindles and machining capacity of over 75 million pieces per year across 26 forging lines
- Customer diversification across 57 customers and geographic diversification supplying more than 17 countries
- Global-approved quality stack (ISO 9001, IATF 16949, ISO 45001, ISO 18001) supporting approvals with global OEMs and bearing majors
- 35 years of operating experience in ring forging, having evolved from a traditional ring forging operation into a diversified, technology-driven precision manufacturer
- Debt-free balance sheet after exiting Corporate Debt Restructuring and settling the Right of Recompense obligation, giving financial flexibility for capacity, technology and customer investment
- Captive renewable energy capacity of 21.55 MW supporting cost position and customer sustainability expectations
bull_bear.title: Bull — competitive strengths

bull_bear.body:
- Demand cyclicality — Fluctuations in demand from automotive, industrial, off-highway and export markets may affect order volumes and capacity utilisation. Mitigated by diversifying across end-use industries, expanding into electric mobility, renewable energy, railways and industrial applications, and strengthening the domestic customer base.
- Customer concentration — Dependence on a limited number of large OEM customers may impact revenue visibility in the event of changes in sourcing strategies. Mitigated by broadening the customer portfolio through new plants of existing customer groups, increasing engagement with global customers, and expanding into new geographies and industry segments.
- Raw material price volatility — Alloy steel is the only commodity used in the manufacturing process; changes in alloy steel prices and input costs, with time-lag constraints on pass-through, can influence profitability and production economics. Inputs tied to global commodity cycles create unpredictable production costs, straining profitability under fixed-price contracts. Mitigated by customer-approved raw material price change mechanisms, long-term procurement arrangements, strategic inventory management, supplier diversification and cost optimisation.
- Export and trade-policy exposure, particularly US tariffs — Global trade uncertainty, especially US tariffs, weighed on legacy bearings and auto component exports through FY26, and export share declined as US tariff uncertainty weighed on volumes. Exports remain a substantial share of turnover, leaving revenue exposed to trade policy and geographic concentration.
- Technology and product development obsolescence — Evolving customer specifications, precision requirements and manufacturing technologies may require continuous capability enhancement. Mitigated by investments in advanced manufacturing technologies, automation, quality systems, process innovation and product development.
- Supply chain disruptions — Interruptions in the supply of critical raw materials or logistics challenges may affect production schedules. Mitigated by developing a diversified supplier base and maintaining appropriate inventory levels.
- Competitive pressure, including low-cost imports and counterfeit product — Cheaper low-cost Chinese imports intensify price competition and compress margins in price-sensitive and aftermarket segments; established industry leaders with entrenched pricing power, superior scale economies and integrated supply chains threaten market share and margin sustainability; and substandard or counterfeit bearings in the replacement segment dilute brand value and undercut authorised players via unorganised channels.
- Skilled workforce availability and attrition in precision manufacturing — Limited availability of skilled operators and controlled manufacturing environments for ISO Grade 3/4 precision bearings needed for EV, aerospace and precision machinery applications. Structural attrition is material, with permanent-worker turnover of 48.34% in FY 2025-26 versus 43.25% in FY 2024-25, and permanent-employee turnover of 14.74% versus 13.26%.
- Automotive OEM demand concentration — With the automotive sector accounting for over 60% of India's bearing demand, revenues remain closely tied to auto production cycles, leaving the business vulnerable to slowdowns in vehicle sales and reduced pricing power during periods of weak OEM offtake.
- Single-location manufacturing concentration — All three manufacturing units are located at Rajkot, Gujarat, with no international plants, concentrating operational, logistics and event risk in a single geography.

outlook.body:
- Global diversification: continued entry into new export geographies, rebalancing toward US, Europe and domestic markets while expanding footprint into high-growth Asia-Pacific and Middle East markets, with premium market access maintained
- Product innovation: launch of advanced machining capabilities, new alloys and co-development with customers, supporting the shift toward higher-value bearing rings and precision components
- Digital transformation: integrated ERP, AI-based quality and maintenance, and end-to-end digital traceability across all three Rajkot manufacturing units, spanning 26 forging lines and 625 machining spindles
- Sustainability: renewable energy capacity at 21.55 MW as of FY26, with continued focus on circular materials, GHG reduction and afforestation initiatives
- Human capital: continued upskilling, safety and inclusive leadership programmes supporting the transition toward higher-precision, higher-margin manufacturing
- Move up the value chain from core ring forging to advanced, precision-engineered assemblies for automotive, EVs, railways and high-performance machinery
- Channel operational excellence into targeted capacity additions, technology upgrades and manufacturing initiatives to drive sustained margin expansion and efficiency
- Redirect financial strength toward long-term stakeholder returns through a debt-free status, healthy net cash position and the shareholder buyback announced in FY26
- EV and industrial diversification as a counterbalance to cyclical ICE-linked automotive demand
outlook.title: Strategy & capital allocation

outlook.body: Rolex Rings operates three manufacturing units, all at Rajkot, Gujarat, with a combined installed forging capacity of 1,65,000 MTPA across 26 forging lines comprising high-speed hot formers and vertical lines, and machining capacity of over 75 million pieces per year on 625 CNC/VMC spindles. During FY26 the Company installed value-added process equipment and added one forging line; capex directed at technologies improving environmental and social impacts rose to 41% of total capex in FY 2025-26 from 34% in FY 2024-25, while R&D investment in such technologies was nil in both years. Management describes channelling operational excellence into funding targeted capacity additions, technology upgrades and manufacturing initiatives to drive sustained margin expansion and efficiency, and is combining processes to move up the value chain from core ring forging to advanced, precision-engineered assemblies for automotive, EVs, railways and high-performance machinery. Digital transformation covers integrated ERP, AI-based quality and maintenance and end-to-end digital traceability across all three Rajkot units. On the energy side the Company has built captive renewable capacity of 21.55 MW as of FY26, comprising a 2.3 MW rooftop solar plant, a 15.5 MW ground-mounted solar power plant and a 3.75 MW windmill power station, and intends to reach 60% renewable energy consumption by 2030 through its own green power generation, subject to government policy and approvals. Having exited CDR and settled its Right of Recompense obligation, the Company states it retains flexibility for future capacity expansion alongside the announced buyback. The annual report does not disclose a named, dated new-plant or greenfield expansion project with a commissioning timeline.
outlook.title: Capex & expansion plans

outlook.body:
- The global automotive sector continues to be a key demand driver, with the Company's EV and industrial diversification providing an increasing counterbalance to cyclical ICE-linked automotive demand
- Improving domestic demand, particularly in bearing rings, and a recovering European market offset a slowdown in US customer volumes pending clarity on the final trade deal
- Bearing rings emerged as the largest and fastest-growing product category, with the mix shifting toward bearing rings as automotive components demand softened globally on rising US tariff rates
- Gross margin expansion driven by disciplined cost management, improved yields and a favourable product mix shift toward higher-value bearing rings
- Margins came under mild pressure owing to exceptional items that arose on a one-time basis and may not impact margins further
- Becoming fully debt-free after settling the RoR obligation freed up cash flow and lowered finance costs, giving management room to announce a shareholder buyback while retaining flexibility for future capacity expansion and working capital
- Structurally high, non-discretionary bearing demand from India's large registered vehicle fleet, with the EV transition accelerating adoption of high-speed, low-friction bearings for motor and e-axle systems
- Industrial automation and PLI-led manufacturing expansion driving precision bearing demand, with rising manufacturing capacity utilisation pointing to continued capex-led demand for industrial-grade bearings
- Railway modernisation, Vande Bharat expansion and freight corridor upgrades generating sustained demand for tapered roller and spherical bearings
- Renewable energy and power infrastructure growth driving demand for large, specialised bearings in wind turbine rotors, generators and gearboxes
- Shift toward smart, sensor-integrated and high-performance bearing technologies pushing customers toward higher-value, higher-margin categories
- Aerospace and defence indigenisation creating new, premium demand for precision forgings the Company could cater to in the upcoming years
- Improved access to capital and a lower cost of compliance following the exit from CDR and the completed Right of Recompense settlement
- Global trade uncertainty, especially US tariffs, weighed on legacy bearings and auto component exports through FY26, cushioned by the growing focus on bearing rings and precision components
- Reducing energy and resource intensity, increasing renewable capacity and minimising waste reinforcing the Company's cost position and alignment with customer sustainability expectations

deepdive.thesis: FY26 revenue flat YoY due to a temporary ~30% US export hit from tariffs, but margins expanded on mix shift to machined components and strong Europe/India growth; with US duties now at 25% and RoR fully settled, FY27 guides to mid-teen growth as US orders resume and European programs ramp.

open.item: The Company announced a share buyback of 1 crore equity shares at Rs 180 per share, aggregating Rs 180 crore and representing 3.67% of total paid-up capital, with promoters indicating their intention not to participate.
The Company announced a Rs 180 crore shareholder buyback in FY26, reinforcing its commitment to disciplined capital allocation and long-term stakeholder returns.
The Company intends to reach 60% consumption from renewable energy by 2030 through its own green power generation, subject to government policy and approvals.
The Company intends to continue moving up the value chain from core ring forging to advanced, precision-engineered assemblies for automotive, EVs, railways and high-performance machinery.

Management flags dependence on a limited number of large OEM customers as a risk to revenue visibility if sourcing strategies change, mitigated by broadening the customer portfolio and expanding into new geographies and industry segments.
The Company is channelling operational excellence into funding targeted capacity additions, technology upgrades and manufacturing initiatives to drive sustained margin expansion and efficiency.
The Company is continuing entry into new export geographies, rebalancing toward US, Europe and domestic markets while expanding its footprint into high-growth Asia-Pacific and Middle East markets.
The Company plants an additional 500+ trees annually, having planted approximately 12,000+ trees over the past five years, contributing to carbon sequestration and ecological restoration.
The Company identifies aerospace and defence indigenisation as an opportunity it can cater to in the upcoming years, creating premium demand for precision forgings.
The Company is funding targeted capacity additions, technology upgrades and manufacturing initiatives to drive sustained margin expansion and efficiency.

risks.note: Fluctuations in demand from automotive, industrial, off-highway and export markets may affect order volumes and capacity utilisation. Mitigated by diversifying across end-use industries, expanding into electric mobility, renewable energy, railways and industrial applications, and strengthening the domestic customer base.

Dependence on a limited number of large OEM customers may impact revenue visibility in the event of changes in sourcing strategies. Mitigated by broadening the customer portfolio through new plants of existing customer groups, increasing engagement with global customers, and expanding into new geographies and industry segments.

Alloy steel is the only commodity used in the manufacturing process; changes in alloy steel prices and input costs, with time-lag constraints on pass-through, can influence profitability and production economics. Inputs tied to global commodity cycles create unpredictable production costs, straining profitability under fixed-price contracts. Mitigated by customer-approved raw material price change mechanisms, long-term procurement arrangements, strategic inventory management, supplier diversification and cost optimisation.

risks.risk: Export and trade-policy exposure, particularly US tariffs
risks.note: Global trade uncertainty, especially US tariffs, weighed on legacy bearings and auto component exports through FY26, and export share declined as US tariff uncertainty weighed on volumes. Exports remain a substantial share of turnover, leaving revenue exposed to trade policy and geographic concentration.

Evolving customer specifications, precision requirements and manufacturing technologies may require continuous capability enhancement. Mitigated by investments in advanced manufacturing technologies, automation, quality systems, process innovation and product development.

Interruptions in the supply of critical raw materials or logistics challenges may affect production schedules. Mitigated by developing a diversified supplier base and maintaining appropriate inventory levels.

risks.risk: Competitive pressure, including low-cost imports and counterfeit product
risks.note: Cheaper low-cost Chinese imports intensify price competition and compress margins in price-sensitive and aftermarket segments; established industry leaders with entrenched pricing power, superior scale economies and integrated supply chains threaten market share and margin sustainability; and substandard or counterfeit bearings in the replacement segment dilute brand value and undercut authorised players via unorganised channels.

risks.risk: Skilled workforce availability and attrition in precision manufacturing
risks.note: Limited availability of skilled operators and controlled manufacturing environments for ISO Grade 3/4 precision bearings needed for EV, aerospace and precision machinery applications. Structural attrition is material, with permanent-worker turnover of 48.34% in FY 2025-26 versus 43.25% in FY 2024-25, and permanent-employee turnover of 14.74% versus 13.26%.

With the automotive sector accounting for over 60% of India's bearing demand, revenues remain closely tied to auto production cycles, leaving the business vulnerable to slowdowns in vehicle sales and reduced pricing power during periods of weak OEM offtake.
All three manufacturing units are located at Rajkot, Gujarat, with no international plants, concentrating operational, logistics and event risk in a single geography.

one-line thesis: FY26 revenue flat YoY due to a temporary ~30% US export hit from tariffs, but margins expanded on mix shift to machined components and strong Europe/India growth; with US duties now at 25% and RoR fully settled, FY27 guides to mid-teen growth as US orders resume and European programs ramp.

demand_drivers.title: Demand & outlook drivers
demand_drivers.body:
- The global automotive sector continues to be a key demand driver, with the Company's EV and industrial diversification providing an increasing counterbalance to cyclical ICE-linked automotive demand
- Improving domestic demand, particularly in bearing rings, and a recovering European market offset a slowdown in US customer volumes pending clarity on the final trade deal
- Bearing rings emerged as the largest and fastest-growing product category, with the mix shifting toward bearing rings as automotive components demand softened globally on rising US tariff rates
- Gross margin expansion driven by disciplined cost management, improved yields and a favourable product mix shift toward higher-value bearing rings
- Margins came under mild pressure owing to exceptional items that arose on a one-time basis and may not impact margins further
- Becoming fully debt-free after settling the RoR obligation freed up cash flow and lowered finance costs, giving management room to announce a shareholder buyback while retaining flexibility for future capacity expansion and working capital
- Structurally high, non-discretionary bearing demand from India's large registered vehicle fleet, with the EV transition accelerating adoption of high-speed, low-friction bearings for motor and e-axle systems
- Industrial automation and PLI-led manufacturing expansion driving precision bearing demand, with rising manufacturing capacity utilisation pointing to continued capex-led demand for industrial-grade bearings
- Railway modernisation, Vande Bharat expansion and freight corridor upgrades generating sustained demand for tapered roller and spherical bearings
- Renewable energy and power infrastructure growth driving demand for large, specialised bearings in wind turbine rotors, generators and gearboxes
- Shift toward smart, sensor-integrated and high-performance bearing technologies pushing customers toward higher-value, higher-margin categories
- Aerospace and defence indigenisation creating new, premium demand for precision forgings the Company could cater to in the upcoming years
- Improved access to capital and a lower cost of compliance following the exit from CDR and the completed Right of Recompense settlement
- Global trade uncertainty, especially US tariffs, weighed on legacy bearings and auto component exports through FY26, cushioned by the growing focus on bearing rings and precision components
- Reducing energy and resource intensity, increasing renewable capacity and minimising waste reinforcing the Company's cost position and alignment with customer sustainability expectations

capex_expansion.title: Capex & expansion plans
capex_expansion.body: Rolex Rings operates three manufacturing units, all at Rajkot, Gujarat, with a combined installed forging capacity of 1,65,000 MTPA across 26 forging lines comprising high-speed hot formers and vertical lines, and machining capacity of over 75 million pieces per year on 625 CNC/VMC spindles. During FY26 the Company installed value-added process equipment and added one forging line; capex directed at technologies improving environmental and social impacts rose to 41% of total capex in FY 2025-26 from 34% in FY 2024-25, while R&D investment in such technologies was nil in both years. Management describes channelling operational excellence into funding targeted capacity additions, technology upgrades and manufacturing initiatives to drive sustained margin expansion and efficiency, and is combining processes to move up the value chain from core ring forging to advanced, precision-engineered assemblies for automotive, EVs, railways and high-performance machinery. Digital transformation covers integrated ERP, AI-based quality and maintenance and end-to-end digital traceability across all three Rajkot units. On the energy side the Company has built captive renewable capacity of 21.55 MW as of FY26, comprising a 2.3 MW rooftop solar plant, a 15.5 MW ground-mounted solar power plant and a 3.75 MW windmill power station, and intends to reach 60% renewable energy consumption by 2030 through its own green power generation, subject to government policy and approvals. Having exited CDR and settled its Right of Recompense obligation, the Company states it retains flexibility for future capacity expansion alongside the announced buyback. The annual report does not disclose a named, dated new-plant or greenfield expansion project with a commissioning timeline.

one-line thesis: FY26 revenue flat YoY due to a temporary ~30% US export hit from tariffs, but margins expanded on mix shift to machined components and strong Europe/India growth; with US duties now at 25% and RoR fully settled, FY27 guides to mid-teen growth as US orders resume and European programs ramp.
financial scorecard: Revenue FY26: INR1,144 cr (flat YoY vs ~INR1,143 cr implied); Gross margin: 49.4%→51.5%; EBITDA margin: >20% maintained; PAT: not explicitly stated in transcript; One-offs: INR22 cr US customs duty expense (partially recoverable from customers, revenue recognition lagged to Q1–Q2 FY27) and INR6 cr legal/professional fees for RoR settlement; Order book: 3–6 month visible, ~INR115–125 cr/month dispatches planned for H1 FY27; Net debt: effectively zero post full RoR payment of INR101 cr on 31-Mar-2026; cash surplus ~INR367 cr.
guidance: Revenue growth: FY27 mid-teen (15–17%), FY28 high-teen or higher; Margins: normalized EBITDA 20.5–21%+, gross margin 49–53% range; Order inflow: US recovery from Q1 FY27, Europe programs ramping to 50–60% of peak in FY27; Capex/commissioning: ~INR30–40 cr/year (maintenance + selective expansions), no major greenfield announced.
order book & pipeline: Program awards typically 5–7 years; near-term visibility 3–6 months; H1 FY27 planned monthly dispatches INR115–125 cr; new European plant programs starting at 10–20% and ramping through FY27; some US programs previously on hold now re-engaging.
segment / subsidiary detail: FY26 split (INR cr): Domestic bearing rings 386; Domestic auto components 170; Export bearing rings 154; Export auto components 350; Scrap 71; Export incentives 13; Total ~1,143. FY25 split (INR cr): Domestic bearing rings 329; Domestic auto components 177; Export bearing rings 155; Export auto components 399; Scrap 78; Export incentives 16. Auto components now ~50%+ of revenue; ~85% of component revenue is machined vs 15% forged-only.
growth verticals / optionality: Europe China+1 wins (60% of new nominations from Europe in FY26); US recovery as tariffs normalize; domestic import substitution in larger bearing rings; early EV/industrial programs; potential new customer programs converting after 15–18 month validation (impact from FY28).
margins & cost dynamics: Gross margin expansion driven by higher-value machined mix and steel sourcing shifts (more domestic); quarterly raw-material pass-through for most overseas customers (some half-yearly); freight/container constraints causing 2–3 week delays and premium costs but manageable via consignment/warehouse inventory.
capex / expansion: ~INR30–40 cr/year anticipated (maintenance + targeted capacity for high-utilization product ranges); FY26 actual capex ~INR36 cr; cold/warm forging not immediate, focused on maximizing hot forging assets.
capital allocation: INR101 cr RoR settlement completed (balance sheet clean, no covenants); Board approved buyback of 1 cr shares at INR180/share (INR180 cr), promoters not participating; open to further dividends but retaining cash for uncertainty and selective capex.
risks & watch-items: US tariff policy volatility (Section 232 at 25% remains); container/freight cost inflation and transit delays; customer inventory rebuild pace; geopolitical disruptions; EV transition timing (currently limited traction vs ICE/hybrid).
management quality / tone: Confident and pragmatic; emphasizes resilience, relationship depth, and balance sheet strength; conservative on recognizing recoverable duty revenues; constructive on FY27 recovery and multi-year ramp.
non-obvious takeaways: INR22 cr customs duty expense booked conservatively in Q4 with corresponding revenue delayed to Q1–Q2 FY27 as customers lift consignment stock; partial refund expected from US government for pre-Nov-2025 IEEPA-related excess duties, which would flow to revenue when received; utilization ~62–63% overall but some product lines at 80–85%, driving targeted capex needs.

| US tariffs spiked to 53% then normalized to 25%, causing temporary 30% drop in US exports and margin pressure from duty costs | ROLEXRINGS | beneficiary | High | Duties now accepted by customers at 25%; management expects meaningful US order recovery from Q1 FY27; one-off duty expense creates near-term PAT noise but cash recovery/refund potential adds upside. |

themes.title: Auto components & EV-driveline localization
themes.need: Premiumization, content-per-vehicle rise and EV/hybrid transition pull a deep auto-ancillary chain - MOTHERSON/SONACOMS/BOSCHLTD/SCHAEFFLER/SKFINDIA/UNOMINDA-tier on driveline, bearings, wiring (MSUMI) and EV systems; OLAELEC/ATHERENERG/OLECTRA on EV OEMs (OLAELEC targeting cell-to-pack 10-15% cost edge); SUNDRMFAST/ENDURANCE/CRAFTSMAN/BHARATFORG on forgings/machining. Q1FY27 showed contracted pricing finally landing for Tier-2s: SSWL earned EBITDA/wheel of Rs 314 against Rs 262 YoY, which management attributed mostly to two years of OEM input-price increases finally landing (1-5%, more pending) rather than mix, with all plants above 95% utilisation and knuckles at 100%; KROSS delivered a 12.23% EBITDA margin (+63bps) BEFORE two retrospective pass-throughs land (steel settled ~15 July, the CV conversion-cost settlement still pending), making Q1 a floor rather than a peak.
themes.driver: GST 2.0 demand pull; retrospective OEM price pass-throughs still to land (KROSS CV conversion cost); EV cell/Gigafactory ramps (OLAELEC 6GWh by June); export + new-platform content wins.

themes.title: Auto OEM cycle - CV replacement & PV premiumization
themes.need: GST 2.0 rate rationalization plus an aged CV fleet still frames the replacement cycle, but Q1FY27's real signal is 2W OEMs EXPANDING margin through a commodity shock. TVSMOTOR sold 1.63mn units (+28%) on INR 13,896cr revenue (+38%) while lifting EBITDA margin 30bps to 12.8% having absorbed a ~4% commodity shock with only ~1.5% of price increase (CARE upgraded it AA+ to AAA), and committed 2W capacity from 6.8mn to 8.3mn by Q4FY27. BAJAJ-AUTO set volume/revenue/EBITDA records with margin at 20.9% (+110bps) through ~4.5% commodity inflation AND ~10% of volume lost to a ransomware shutdown, with EV now 30% of domestic revenue at double-digit EBITDA and Chetak EBITDA-positive - a scaled, profitable EV second engine. Commercial mobility is electrifying fastest: TVSMOTOR's 3W EV penetration crossed 40% for the first time. ASHOKLEY's all-time-high CV volumes (220k units, MHCV share 30.8%) carry the CV leg with defence + Switch EV optionality; TMCV/TMPV/SMLMAH/ESCORTS on CV/tractors; APOLLOTYRE/JKTYRE/BALKRISIND/MRF on tyres.
themes.driver: Capacity commissioning against demand (TVSMOTOR 2W to 8.3mn by Q4FY27, BAJAJ-AUTO 7m to 9m+ units); 3W/2W EV penetration inflection; GST-2.0 price-cut demand, aged-fleet replacement and festive 2W/PV.
